--- title: "Candy Mini-Project" author: Quinn Nemeth format: html toc: TRUE --- ## Exploring the Data Read in the data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candy_file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv" candy = read.csv(candy_file, row.names=1) head(candy) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chocolate fruity caramel peanutyalmondy nougat crispedricewafer 100 Grand 1 0 1 0 0 1 3 Musketeers 1 0 0 0 1 0 One dime 0 0 0 0 0 0 One quarter 0 0 0 0 0 0 Air Heads 0 1 0 0 0 0 Almond Joy 1 0 0 1 0 0 hard bar pluribus sugarpercent pricepercent winpercent 100 Grand 0 1 0 0.732 0.860 66.97173 3 Musketeers 0 1 0 0.604 0.511 67.60294 One dime 0 0 0 0.011 0.116 32.26109 One quarter 0 0 0 0.011 0.511 46.11650 Air Heads 0 0 0 0.906 0.511 52.34146 Almond Joy 0 1 0 0.465 0.767 50.34755 ``` ::: ::: > Q1. How many different candy types are in this dataset? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(candy) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 85 ``` ::: ::: > Q2. How many fruity candy types are in the dataset? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(candy$fruity) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 38 ``` ::: ::: Analyzing `winpercent`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candy["Twix", ]$winpercent ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 81.64291 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Attaching package: 'dplyr' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': filter, lag ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following objects are masked from 'package:base': intersect, setdiff, setequal, union ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} candy |> filter(row.names(candy)=="Twix") |> select(winpercent) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` winpercent Twix 81.64291 ``` ::: ::: > Q3. What is your favorite candy (other than Twix) in the dataset and what is it’s `winpercent` value? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candy["Almond Joy", ]$winpercent ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 50.34755 ``` ::: ::: > Q4. What is the `winpercent` value for “Kit Kat”? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candy["Kit Kat", ]$winpercent ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 76.7686 ``` ::: ::: > Q5. What is the `winpercent` value for “Tootsie Roll Snack Bars”? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} candy["Tootsie Roll Snack Bars", ]$winpercent ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 49.6535 ``` ::: ::: Using `skim()` from the `skimr` package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library("skimr") skim(candy) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Data summary | | | |:------------------------|:-----| |Name |candy | |Number of rows |85 | |Number of columns |12 | |_______________________ | | |Column type frequency: | | |numeric |12 | |________________________ | | |Group variables |None | **Variable type: numeric** |skim_variable | n_missing| complete_rate| mean| sd| p0| p25| p50| p75| p100|hist | |:----------------|---------:|-------------:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|:-----| |chocolate | 0| 1| 0.44| 0.50| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▆ | |fruity | 0| 1| 0.45| 0.50| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▆ | |caramel | 0| 1| 0.16| 0.37| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▂ | |peanutyalmondy | 0| 1| 0.16| 0.37| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▂ | |nougat | 0| 1| 0.08| 0.28| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▁ | |crispedricewafer | 0| 1| 0.08| 0.28| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▁ | |hard | 0| 1| 0.18| 0.38| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▂ | |bar | 0| 1| 0.25| 0.43| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▂ | |pluribus | 0| 1| 0.52| 0.50| 0.00| 0.00| 1.00| 1.00| 1.00|▇▁▁▁▇ | |sugarpercent | 0| 1| 0.48| 0.28| 0.01| 0.22| 0.47| 0.73| 0.99|▇▇▇▇▆ | |pricepercent | 0| 1| 0.47| 0.29| 0.01| 0.26| 0.47| 0.65| 0.98|▇▇▇▇▆ | |winpercent | 0| 1| 50.32| 14.71| 22.45| 39.14| 47.83| 59.86| 84.18|▃▇▆▅▂ | ::: ::: > Q6. Is there any variable/column that looks to be on a different scale to the majority of the other columns in the dataset? Yes, it looks like the last three columns are all representing percentages, differing from the other 9 that are all binary (1/0). The `winpercent` column in particular is written in % form rather than decimal form (i.e., 50 instead of 0.50), so it has much larger values than any other column. > Q7. What do you think a zero and one represent for the candy$chocolate column? The 0 represents that there are zero observations missing. The 1 represents that all observations are present/observations are present for 100% of rows. ## Exploratory Analysis > Q8. Plot a histogram of winpercent values using both base R and ggplot2. Base R: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(candy$winpercent) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ggplot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) ggplot(candy, aes(x = winpercent)) + geom_histogram(bins = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q9. Is the distribution of winpercent values symmetrical? The center of the distribution is slightly shifted to the left to around 40%. As a result, the distribution is somewhat asymmetrical with bias towards lower values. > Q10. Is the center of the distribution above or below 50%? The center is *below* 50%. > Q11. On average is chocolate candy higher or lower ranked than fruit candy? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chocolatepercent <- candy$winpercent[as.logical(candy$chocolate)] fruitypercent <- candy$winpercent[as.logical(candy$fruity)] meanchoc <- mean(chocolatepercent) meanfru <- mean(fruitypercent) meanchoc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 60.92153 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} meanfru ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 44.11974 ``` ::: ::: Chocolate candy is, on average, **higher** ranked than fruit candy. > Q12. Is this difference statistically significant? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(x = chocolatepercent, y = fruitypercent) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: chocolatepercent and fruitypercent t = 6.2582, df = 68.882, p-value = 2.871e-08 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 11.44563 22.15795 sample estimates: mean of x mean of y 60.92153 44.11974 ``` ::: ::: The different *is* statistically significant. ## Overall Candy Rankings > Q13. What are the five least liked candy types in this set? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) leastliked <- candy %>% arrange(winpercent) head(leastliked) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chocolate fruity caramel peanutyalmondy nougat Nik L Nip 0 1 0 0 0 Boston Baked Beans 0 0 0 1 0 Chiclets 0 1 0 0 0 Super Bubble 0 1 0 0 0 Jawbusters 0 1 0 0 0 Root Beer Barrels 0 0 0 0 0 crispedricewafer hard bar pluribus sugarpercent pricepercent Nik L Nip 0 0 0 1 0.197 0.976 Boston Baked Beans 0 0 0 1 0.313 0.511 Chiclets 0 0 0 1 0.046 0.325 Super Bubble 0 0 0 0 0.162 0.116 Jawbusters 0 1 0 1 0.093 0.511 Root Beer Barrels 0 1 0 1 0.732 0.069 winpercent Nik L Nip 22.44534 Boston Baked Beans 23.41782 Chiclets 24.52499 Super Bubble 27.30386 Jawbusters 28.12744 Root Beer Barrels 29.70369 ``` ::: ::: The five *least* liked candy types in this set are Nik L Nip, Boston Baked Beans, Chiclets, Super Bubble, and Jawbusters. > Q14. What are the top 5 all time favorite candy types out of this set? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mostliked <- candy %>% arrange(desc(winpercent)) head(mostliked) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chocolate fruity caramel peanutyalmondy nougat Reese's Peanut Butter cup 1 0 0 1 0 Reese's Miniatures 1 0 0 1 0 Twix 1 0 1 0 0 Kit Kat 1 0 0 0 0 Snickers 1 0 1 1 1 Reese's pieces 1 0 0 1 0 crispedricewafer hard bar pluribus sugarpercent Reese's Peanut Butter cup 0 0 0 0 0.720 Reese's Miniatures 0 0 0 0 0.034 Twix 1 0 1 0 0.546 Kit Kat 1 0 1 0 0.313 Snickers 0 0 1 0 0.546 Reese's pieces 0 0 0 1 0.406 pricepercent winpercent Reese's Peanut Butter cup 0.651 84.18029 Reese's Miniatures 0.279 81.86626 Twix 0.906 81.64291 Kit Kat 0.511 76.76860 Snickers 0.651 76.67378 Reese's pieces 0.651 73.43499 ``` ::: ::: The five *most* liked candy types in this set are Reese's Peanut Butter cup, Reese's Miniatures, Twix, Kit Kat, and Snickers. > Q15. Make a first barplot of candy ranking based on winpercent values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(candy, aes(winpercent, rownames(candy))) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q16. This is quite ugly, use the reorder() function to get the bars sorted by winpercent? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(candy, aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy), winpercent))) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Add some color: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_cols=rep("black", 85) my_cols[as.logical(candy$chocolate)] = "chocolate" my_cols[as.logical(candy$bar)] = "brown" my_cols[as.logical(candy$fruity)] = "lightpink" ggplot(candy) + aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy),winpercent)) + geom_col(fill=my_cols) + ylab("") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q17. What is the worst ranked chocolate candy? The worst ranked chocolate candy is Sixlets. > Q18. What is the best ranked fruity candy? The best ranked fruity candy is Starburst. ## Analyzing `pricepercent` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggrepel) my_cols[as.logical(candy$fruity)] = "red" ggplot(candy) + aes(x = winpercent, y = pricepercent, label = rownames(candy)) + geom_point(col = my_cols) + geom_text_repel(col = my_cols, size = 3.3, max.overlaps = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q19. Which candy type is the highest ranked in terms of winpercent for the least money - i.e. offers the most bang for your buck? Based on the figure, Reese's Miniatures is the highest ranked candy below `pricepercent = 50`. It has a win rate over 80% with a price point of only 0.279 (27.9%). > Q20. What are the top 5 most expensive candy types in the dataset and of these which is the least popular? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} expensive <- candy %>% arrange(desc(pricepercent)) head(expensive) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chocolate fruity caramel peanutyalmondy nougat Nik L Nip 0 1 0 0 0 Nestle Smarties 1 0 0 0 0 Ring pop 0 1 0 0 0 Hershey's Krackel 1 0 0 0 0 Hershey's Milk Chocolate 1 0 0 0 0 Hershey's Special Dark 1 0 0 0 0 crispedricewafer hard bar pluribus sugarpercent Nik L Nip 0 0 0 1 0.197 Nestle Smarties 0 0 0 1 0.267 Ring pop 0 1 0 0 0.732 Hershey's Krackel 1 0 1 0 0.430 Hershey's Milk Chocolate 0 0 1 0 0.430 Hershey's Special Dark 0 0 1 0 0.430 pricepercent winpercent Nik L Nip 0.976 22.44534 Nestle Smarties 0.976 37.88719 Ring pop 0.965 35.29076 Hershey's Krackel 0.918 62.28448 Hershey's Milk Chocolate 0.918 56.49050 Hershey's Special Dark 0.918 59.23612 ``` ::: ::: The top 5 most expensive candy types are Nik L Nip, Nestle Smarties, Ring Pop, Hershey's Krackel, and Hershey's Milk Chocolate. Of these, Nik L Nip is the least popular. ## Correlation Structure ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(corrplot) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` corrplot 0.95 loaded ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cij <- cor(candy) corrplot(cij) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q22. Examining this plot what two variables are anti-correlated (i.e. have minus values)? Chocolate and fruity are the most strongly anti-correlated pair. Other, less-strongly anti-correlated pairs include: - Fruity & bar - Pluribus & bar - Pricepercent & fruity - Peanutyalmondy & fruity - Winpercent & fruity - Etc. > Q23. Use your corrplot result to make a prediction: which variables do you expect will have the largest contributions (i.e. loadings) to PC1 (i.e., drive the most separation between candies along the first principal component)? I expect that chocolate and fruity will drive the most separation in PC1, because they are the most strongly anti-correlated. This will drive separation of the data into distinct clusters. ## Principal Component Analysis ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca <- prcomp(candy, scale = TRUE) summary(pca) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Importance of components: PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4 PC5 PC6 PC7 Standard deviation 2.0788 1.1378 1.1092 1.07533 0.9518 0.81923 0.81530 Proportion of Variance 0.3601 0.1079 0.1025 0.09636 0.0755 0.05593 0.05539 Cumulative Proportion 0.3601 0.4680 0.5705 0.66688 0.7424 0.79830 0.85369 PC8 PC9 PC10 PC11 PC12 Standard deviation 0.74530 0.67824 0.62349 0.43974 0.39760 Proportion of Variance 0.04629 0.03833 0.03239 0.01611 0.01317 Cumulative Proportion 0.89998 0.93832 0.97071 0.98683 1.00000 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(pca$x) + aes(x = PC1, y = PC2) + geom_point(col = my_cols) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_data <- cbind(candy, pca$x) p <- ggplot(my_data) + aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, size = winpercent/100, text = rownames(my_data), label = rownames(my_data)) + geom_point(col = my_cols) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q24. Complete the code to generate the “Halloween Candy PCA Space Map” above. Be sure to have legible labels along with a plot title and subtitle: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p + geom_text_repel(size=3.3, col=my_cols, max.overlaps = 7) + theme(legend.position = "none") + labs(label = rownames(candy), title = "Halloween Candy PCA Space", subtitle = "Colored by type: chocolate bar (dark brown), chocolate other(light brown), fruity (red), other (black)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(plotly) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Attaching package: 'plotly' ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following object is masked from 'package:ggplot2': last_plot ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following object is masked from 'package:stats': filter ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` The following object is masked from 'package:graphics': layout ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ggplotly(p) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: > Q25. Complete the code to generate the loadings plot above. What original variables are picked up strongly by PC1 in the positive direction? Do these make sense to you? Where did you see this relationship highlighted previously? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(pca$rotation) + aes(PC1, reorder(colnames(candy), PC1)) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The variables picked up strongly in the positive direction were `fruity`, `pluribus`, and `hard`. In the correlation plot, `pluribus` and `hard` were the only two variables that `fruity` was positively correlated with, so it makes sense that they would be grouped together. It also makes sense with general knowledge/intuitively-- fruit candy is more likely to have these two traits than others like `caramel` or `nougat`. > Q26. Based on your exploratory analysis, correlation findings, and PCA results, what combination of characteristics appears to make a “winning” candy? How do these different analyses (visualization, correlation, PCA) support or complement each other in reaching this conclusion? In the plot of `winpercent`, we can see that chocolate candy tends to be on top of the graph/have higher popularity than non-chocolate candy. In the correlation plot, we can see that `chocolate` and `fruity` are strongly anticorrelated, and that they seem to each be positively correlated with a *separate* set of variables. Therefore, we can expect to see two distinct groups/clusters in our PCA analysis. Then, looking at our PCA plot, we can in fact see a clear separation of chocolate and fruit candy. In addition, the chocolate candy seems to have separated into two groups as well-- bar and non-bar. In the loadings plot, we can then see which side of the plot `winpercent` is associated with, and other variables that are associated with the same side. `winpercent` strongly influences points towards the negative/left side of the plot. More negative numbers are also strongly associated with `chocolate` and `bar`. This indicates that a "winning" candy tends to be a type of chocolate bar. ## PCA from Scratch Read in the mystery dataset: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- read.csv("mystery.csv") head(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y z 1 40.6 28.3 -1.1 2 40.1 30.4 -1.1 3 40.7 31.1 -1.1 4 42.0 30.4 -1.1 5 43.5 28.3 -1.1 6 37.5 28.3 14.5 ``` ::: ::: Visualize with a 3D scatterplot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(scatterplot3d) scatterplot3d(m) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q27. Hmm… can you tell what the mystery dataset represents from this 3D plot? Hint: It is something that goes well with chocolate in Barry’s opnion. It doesn't really seem possible to tell just from the plot. It's not clear to me yet what this data represents. Compute the covariance matrix: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cij <- cov(m) cij ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x y z x 2036.5727580 134.9131571 -0.2923907 y 134.9131571 761.6970573 0.0343026 z -0.2923907 0.0343026 553.4070615 ``` ::: ::: Eigen decomposition of covariance matrix: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ans <- eigen(cij) eigenval <- ans$values # variance captured by each PC eigenvec <- ans$vectors # the new axes (principal components) ``` ::: How much variance does each PC capture? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(cumsum(eigenval) / sum(eigenval) * 100, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 61.18 83.49 100.00 ``` ::: ::: > Q28. What percentage of the total variance is captured by the first two principal components together? Does this seem like enough to get a meaningful 2D representation of a 3D object? Together, the first two PCs capture 83.49% of the variance. This seems like a reasonably sufficient amount to get a meaningful 2D visualization. Now, set up & create the 2D plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Step 3: Project data onto the top 2 eigenvectors scores <- as.matrix(m) %*% eigenvec[, 1:2] # Set some colnames for easier plotting colnames(scores) <- c("PC1", "PC2") ggplot(scores) + aes(PC1, PC2) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q29. What is the mystery dataset? Does it make sense that PCA was able to recover a recognizable 2D view from 3D data? What has been “lost” in the reduction from 3D to 2D? It maybe looks like some kind of cup-- maybe a cup of tea? It does make sense that PCA was able to recover something recognizable. In the reduction, it lost the 3-dimensionality that was making the visualization hard to understand. You do lose some information about the data, but you can better understand what's left. Verify with `prcomp()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- prcomp(m) summary(p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Importance of components: PC1 PC2 PC3 Standard deviation 45.2846 27.3418 23.5246 Proportion of Variance 0.6118 0.2230 0.1651 Cumulative Proportion 0.6118 0.8349 1.0000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(p$x) + aes(PC1, PC2) + geom_point(size=2, col="steelblue", alpha=0.5) + labs(title="Mystery dataset: PCA projection", subtitle="3D structure recovered in 2D") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](class10bggn213_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: > Q30. Do the results from prcomp() match your manual eigen decomposition? The scores may differ in sign (direction) — this is normal and does not affect interpretation. Why do you think this is? It looks like the manual version plotted the data upside-down-- now, in the correct direction, it is clear that the data is representing a teapot. However, even though the plot from before had a different sign, it still matches the same shape as in the `prcomp()` version. Maybe this could be because it's random whether a particular set of traits is assigned to one end of the PC axis or another. I.e., negative and positive could be swapped and the same variation would still be represented.
